one_liner: Small Rust buffered reader returning borrowed line slices; beats std BufRead::read_until and lines() for byte-oriented line scanning.
what_it_does: LineReader wraps any io::Read and hands out &[u8] slices of its own fixed internal buffer (64 KiB default, configurable delimiter and capacity) instead of copying into a caller Vec. It is a different interface, not a BufRead drop-in: next_line() returns Option<io::Result<&[u8]>> with the delimiter included, next_batch() returns every complete line currently in the buffer as one slice, and for_each() runs a closure per line.
how_it_is_fast: It avoids per-line copying and allocation by borrowing from a fixed buffer, and finds delimiters with the memchr crate (memchr for the next line, memrchr to find the last complete line after each read). next_batch() skips per-line splitting entirely, so a caller with its own SIMD or parallel scanner gets whole blocks of complete lines at near raw read() speed; refill only moves the trailing partial line to the buffer start.
when_to_use: Scanning large log or text files line by line as bytes (no UTF-8 validation needed) where read_until plus buf.clear() is the hot loop
Pipelines that can process many lines at once: next_batch() hands out multi-line blocks for your own memchr/SIMD parsing or for passing to worker threads
Inputs with a known maximum line length that fits comfortably within the buffer (configure with with_capacity)
Non-newline record separators such as NUL or tab via with_delimiter
when_not_to_use: Inputs with unbounded line length: lines longer than the buffer are silently split and you cannot tell a truncated line from a final line without a newline (open issue #3)
Code that needs owned Strings or UTF-8 validated lines: you must copy and validate yourself, which erodes the per-line gain
New projects that want maintained code: unmaintained since 2019 (v0.4.0); the author points to bstr for_byte_line (0.2.8+) as performing similarly without the line-length limit
Expecting the 7x headline per line: like-for-like next_line() was 1.51 s vs read_until 1.94 s (1.28x) on the README run

integration.min_toolchain: not documented (Rust 2015 edition, extern crate syntax)
integration.thread_safety: Single reader object with &mut self methods; returned slices borrow the reader, so it is not shared across threads (issue #1 on thread-friendly batching still open)

gotchas: Returned slices borrow the reader's buffer and are invalidated by the next call, so collecting lines requires to_vec()
Lines longer than the buffer come back as several pieces, and the only hint is the missing trailing delimiter
Using get_mut() on the inner reader without reset() desynchronizes buffered state
When the leftover fragment is longer than the consumed part, refill uses Vec::drain plus extend with a fresh zeroed Vec, an allocation on that path
pick_this_over_siblings_when: rawscan is the closest sibling (C, beats fgets/getline on CPU time); pick linereader inside Rust code for byte-line scanning, and rawscan for C/C++ programs. For a maintained Rust option compare against bstr's for_byte_line before adopting this.
verified_claims_summary: The author's README run on a 976 MB, 10.3M-line XML file (Westmere Xeon 2.1 GHz, FreeBSD/ZFS, compiler and harness not published) measured next_batch 0.27 s vs raw read() 0.25 s, next_line 1.51 s, std read_until 1.94 s, read_line 2.54 s and lines() 3.23 s; a second run recorded in src/lib.rs on a 31.6 GB, 501.6M-line input gave LineReader 407.52 MB/s vs read_until 252.62 MB/s (1.61x, derived from page data). The std BufReader capacity used for the baselines is not stated, versus LineReader's 64 KiB buffer.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-09-13 (v0.4.0 on crates.io, about 2.0M downloads, about 289k recent), but MIT-licensed, about 400 lines with no unsafe code and a single memchr dependency, so it is easy to vendor.
